paras: The stoning of the Lincoln School teachers' home was a mob attack on the night of Thursday, September 10, 1903, on the house occupied by the teachers of Lincoln school, a school for Black children in Meridian, Mississippi. Stones smashed several shutters and windows while the principal, Mrs. H. I. Miller of Topeka, Kansas, stayed inside, and no one was reported hurt. Kansas papers carried the story because of Miller's Topeka ties, linking the attack to a Meridian Star editorial and to President Roosevelt's friendship with Booker T. Washington.

Lincoln school was described as a colored school with about 500 pupils, run under the auspices of the American Missionary Association of New York and organized by Miller as the first school of its kind in Meridian. Miller had spent the summer in Topeka and left in early August to resume work as principal. According to the Topeka State Journal, the Meridian Star had opposed the school since its founding and had printed violent editorials over Roosevelt's stance on "the negro question." On the Wednesday night before the attack, the Star ran a "double-leaded editorial" urging the city to drive out northerners teaching colored schools.

The following night a mob stoned the teachers' home at 2705 Eleventh street, some distance from the school building and chapel. School had not yet opened, and Miller, who had come early to prepare the buildings, was the only teacher in the house. By her account she kept indoors out of range of the stones, and the attackers dispersed once they "grew tired of stoning the house."

The next day the Star printed what the Topeka paper called a "flaring account," stating that the principal had dashed out and fired several shots at the mob. In a letter to Topeka friends, Miller said she had written to the mayor of Meridian asking for protection and believed the school would not be molested. No report of arrests or of a reply from the mayor appears in the coverage. Miller was still principal in July 1904, when she lectured on the school in Vermont.

The Topeka State Journal ran the fullest story on September 14 under the headline "Stoned Her School," putting "southern gentlemen" in quotation marks, calling the attackers "cowardly rioters" and the Star a "niggerhating" paper, and likening Meridian to Pekin under the Boxers. Four days later the Kansas Agitator condensed the story into one paragraph among its news notes, describing an attack on the school itself and attributing it to Roosevelt's attitude toward Booker T. Washington.

Mississippi coverage of the attack itself was not found, though on October 1 the Brandon News reprinted an Alabama paper's support for the Star's complaint about the school's "northern white women" teachers, which said such institutions should be "abated as a nuisance." No Black-press report of the attack was found.

Accounts differ on Miller's conduct: the Star, as summarized in Topeka, said she fired on the crowd, while the Topeka paper said she did nothing but stay indoors. The Kansas Agitator described the school as the target, but the Topeka report placed the attack at the teachers' home, away from the school grounds' main buildings.

reader.title: Stoning of the Lincoln School teachers' home, Meridian, Mississippi
bases: A mob stoned and damaged the house of the northern teachers of a colored school the night after a Meridian Star editorial urged driving such teachers out; no one was hurt and no threat to kill is reported (A2, A3).

Both reports come from Kansas and rest on Mrs. Miller's own account to Topeka friends; the brief Kansas Agitator item (A3) follows the Topeka State Journal story (A2) closely and adds no independent detail beyond its stated cause, and no Mississippi or Black-press report of the attack was found.
